title: Judge Loop and Modular Tests
eyebrow: house-rules · fix proposal · nothing built yet
approval: Design approved: judge blocking fix and modular tests

short.lead: The end-of-reply judge blocked 12 times in a row, and the long waits behind it come from tests that run as one slow block. I propose two linked fixes: stop the judge looping and tell the model which reply passes, and force tests into independent modules that each run in under a minute and print their own result, with a reusable skill that converts existing tests.
short.hint: Tap a step to see what it changes. The choices at the end are yours.

items: You pick the choices and approve
I record a dated entry in docs/6-decisions/Decisions.md and write a build plan.

changes: new
What exists today
Three checks run on every Stop, and they do not know about each other.

The model judge (the Stop entry of type prompt in hooks.json) reads only the last reply, keeps no count, and always answers "try three different methods and list them", even when the reply already did. The phrase and record check (scripts/house_rules/core.py, roadblock_check) blocks at most twice per user message. The goal check (same file, _goal_check) blocks up to six times on its own counter. The counters live in separate files, so nothing limits the total number of blocks. I looked for the transcript of the blocked session by listing the newest transcripts, searching them for the judge's wording, and reading the counter files and the hook log. I found only synthetic test transcripts, so I have not reproduced the 12 blocks. Every live counter file stops at 2, which points at the uncapped model judge.
Three Stop checks with caps of none, 2 and 6.
Nothing yet.
Your test run was blocked 12 times.
cut
Delete the model judge
It repeats what the two scripted checks already do, cannot count its own blocks, and cannot see the tool history.

A prompt hook cannot keep state, so it cannot be capped. The record check already reads the real transcript and is the better judge of whether three methods were tried. Deleting the hooks.json entry removes the only uncapped block. The verify.py test case for issue #591 (core.py:1477) currently checks that the entry exists. I change it to check that the entry is gone.
The hooks.json Stop prompt hook.
The entry is removed.
No more unlimited blocks.
adapt
One shared cap
The record check and the goal check share one counter, which allows two blocks per user message.

After two blocks the reply goes out with a visible warning, as the record check does today. The counter resets only when the turn made at least one real tool call after the last block, so a model that keeps working is checked again, while a model that only rewords its reply is not blocked a third time.
Two counters with caps 2 and 6.
One counter with cap 2.
The worst case is two blocks, not twelve.
adapt
Fewer false alarms
Stop treating ordinary words as roadblocks.

The words "next step" are removed from the stall list, because the house rules themselves tell every reply to end with one next step. The claim list drops the bare phrases "could not", "unable to" and "I can't", and keeps phrases about a missing tool, machine or access. A reply with a NEEDS YOU line is exempt from the goal check too.
_STALL_RE and _ROADBLOCK_RE in core.py.
Narrower lists, and NEEDS YOU exempts both checks.
Normal status replies pass.
new
The passing reply, spelled out
The block message includes the exact lines to paste.

Each block names the claim it matched (quoted), what is missing, how many blocks remain, and one of four accepted forms: a Roadblock record of three numbered methods with what each returned, a No other method line with the reason, a NEEDS YOU line, or a Goal status line. The record is still checked against the real failed tool calls, so invented methods do not pass. The same forms are written into rules/detail/roadblocks.md so the model knows them before it is blocked.
Messages say only to try three methods.
Messages carry a copyable accepted reply.
The model can always find the way out.
new
Tests: the approved design already exists
Another session on your other account designed modular tests, and you approved it on 2026-11-23.

The design is docs/4-systems/modular-tests.md, tracked as issue 575 with children 576 to 582 (rule text, a refactor on and off switch, a write-time gate that refuses non-modular tests, a skill and audit, converting tools/verify_tools.py, one issue per offshoot suite, and docs). It is not built yet. I will extend it, not redo it. It already gives every module a name and a run-alone command, chaining through a --parts runner, and a conversion skill with a proof that old and new runs report the same checks. I measured the plugin's own core part at 68.9 seconds, already over the 60-second target, and one of its 267 checks fails (the injected rules are 9721 characters against a 9700 limit); that failure was there before this proposal and is a separate item.
Design approved, nothing built, issues 575 to 582 open.
Three additions to that design, below.
No duplicate design; one set of issues.
new
Addition 1: a 60-second budget
Any module or run that needs over a minute is flagged and must be split.

Your design does not set a time limit yet. This adds one line to the module header, a measured time recorded after each run, and a flag listing every module over 60 seconds with its name and time. The 60 comes from rules/waits.json, so it changes in one place. A step that truly cannot split, such as one engine build, passes with one line: Cannot split: followed by the reason. That line uses the shared cap from the judge fix, so it cannot loop. It lands in the gate (issue 578) and the audit (issue 579).
A 60-second foreground limit exists; no module time is recorded.
A measured flag with a named way out.
A slow module is found and split before it blocks a session.
adapt
Addition 2: each module prints its own result, as it finishes
Results appear per module, in the order they finish.

The approved header names a module and its run-alone command, but does not require the module to print its own PASS or FAIL and a RESULT line. This adds that requirement to the gate. It also changes verify.py, which today prints each part only when its turn in the fixed order comes, so a finished part waits behind a slower one. The change prints each part the moment it ends.
verify.py holds finished output until earlier parts end.
Each module prints when done.
You and the model see results sooner.
new
Addition 3: proof that modules are independent
The conversion skill runs each module alone, then all in shuffled order.

Your design proves that old and new runs report the same checks. That does not prove independence, because a fixed order can hide a module that needs another one's leftovers. This adds a second proof to /house-rules:modular-tests convert: run each module alone, then all modules in a shuffled order, and compare. A mismatch is reported as a hidden link and not auto-fixed.
The proof compares counts only.
Counts plus alone-and-shuffled runs.
A hidden dependency is caught during conversion.
risk
Flaws I found in this design
Four known gaps, each with its answer.

One: deleting the model judge means roadblock wording that the phrase list misses is no longer caught. I accept this, because the goal check still covers unattended runs. Two: a model could write fake methods, so the record is checked against real failed tool calls. Three: a shared cap of two with no reset would leave a long unattended run unchecked, so the cap resets after real tool work. Four: I have not confirmed whether Claude Code's own limit of 8 consecutive blocks applies to prompt hooks. Beyond the missing cap, the 12 is unexplained, so the build plan adds a replay of a real session to check.
None of these gaps is handled today.
Each gap has a test or a stated limit.
You see the limits before approving.
risk
Flaws I found in the test design
Four known gaps, each with its answer.

One: speed differs by machine, so the time is measured on the machine running it and recorded, not assumed. Two: a split can hide a real dependency; the shuffled run is the proof, and a failure is reported, not fixed silently. Three: one engine build may never fit in 60 seconds; the Cannot split line is the exit. Four: the 12-block loop came from a judge, so every new refusal here needs the shared cap and a copyable accepted reply, or it would repeat the same fault.
Nothing guards against these today.
Each gap has a test or a stated limit.
You see the limits before approving.
choices: first
What should happen to the model judge?
A
Delete it
It cannot be capped and the scripted checks cover the same ground.
B
Keep it, run only when the scripted checks pass
It would still be uncapped, and it would add a delay to every reply.
C
Replace it with a scripted call that is cap-aware
This needs more code and gives the same result as deleting it.
Deleting is the shortest change and removes the only uncapped block.
share
What should the shared cap be?
A
Two blocks, reset after real tool work
Matches today's record check. The blocks are limited, but long unattended runs are still checked.
B
Two blocks per user message, no reset
Simplest, but an unattended run is no longer checked after two blocks.
C
Three blocks
One more block per reply, so the loop could run one step longer.
A cap of two with a reset ends the loop and still checks long unattended runs.
flask
Where should the 60-second flag live?
A
Inside the approved gate and audit (issues 578 and 579)
One refusal path, one way out, and no second checker to keep in step.
B
A separate checker, tests_budget.py
Cleaner to test alone, but a second place that blocks.
The approved design already has the gate and the audit, so the flag belongs there.

wrapup.summary: A proposal with two linked parts: stop the end-of-reply judge looping, and force tests into independent modules that finish within a minute.
wrapup.changing: Nothing is built. It would edit hooks.json, scripts/house_rules/core.py, rules/detail/roadblocks.md and verify.py, and extend the approved modular-tests design (issues 575 to 582) with a time budget, per-module results and an independence proof.
wrapup.blocking: Your approval and your three choices: the model judge, the shared cap, and where the 60-second flag lives.
